paragraphs.text: MEHMO syndrome is an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome. Its name comes from its cardinal features: mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity. In the family originally reported, patients did not live beyond 2 years (Steinmuller et al., 1998; DeLozier-Blanchet et al., 1999).

paragraphs.text: Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) described 2 brothers with a severe syndrome of postnatal growth retardation and mental retardation. Features included extreme microcephaly, obesity developing during infancy, microgonadism, and a characteristic amphora-shaped facies. The neurologic examination was highly abnormal, with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, and extremely irritable and agitated behavior. The first child also had neonatal hypoglycemia and chronic constipation, and he died at age 4.5 years. The authors noted that the brothers most resembled patients with Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome (BFL). However, the dwarfism and mental retardation were much more severe than in any reported BFL patient, and the neurologic and dysmorphic features differed significantly. They considered 2 possibilities: a particularly severe, perhaps allelic, variant of BFL, or a previously undescribed disorder.

paragraphs.text: Borck et al. (2012) reported a family of Moroccan Jewish ancestry in the maternal line in which 3 males had an intellectual disability syndrome with apparent X-linked inheritance. Common features were moderate to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, and facial dysmorphism. Each affected individual also had unique features. Individual III:1 had cleft lip and palate and behavioral impairments. Individual III:2 had generalized seizures, and brain MRI at age 1 year showed a very thin corpus callosum, microcephaly, and mild enlargement and asymmetry of the lateral ventricles. Individual II:3 had postpubertal microgenitalism and obesity.

paragraphs.text: Skopkova et al. (2017) reported 4 families with MEHMO syndrome. The first index patient (family 1) was a boy born to nonconsanguineous Slovak parents and had a healthy older sister. Microcephaly was detected prenatally at 28 weeks' gestation. He developed partial complex seizures at age 4 months, which were resistant to anticonvulsants, and MEHMO was diagnosed at 10 months. He had severe mental and motor delay, micropenis, cryptorchidism, central obesity, dysphagia, central hypotonia with peripheral hypertonia, and short stature. Dysmorphic features included full cheeks, large ears, downturned corners of the mouth, epiblepharon, long eyelashes, thick eyebrows, tapered fingers, and talipes. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination, cerebral atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum. Other findings included: - neonatal hypoglycemia - non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus treated with insulin from age 10 months - panhypopituitarism - atrial septal defect - elevated hepatic enzymes - severe combined dyslipidemia - recurrent bronchitis and bronchopneumonia - abnormal muscle mitochondria with decreased activity of respiratory chain complex II He was last reported at age 5 years. During intercurrent illness his condition worsened markedly, with more seizures and poorer diabetes control, which the authors compared to vanishing white matter disease.

paragraphs.text: Family 3 of Skopkova et al. (2017) was the German family previously reported by Steinmuller et al. (1998), with 4 affected males. The index patient (IV:3) was diagnosed prenatally with microcephaly. Therapy-resistant epileptic seizures were diagnosed at age 7 weeks. All affected males had the following features: - microcephaly and therapy-resistant seizures - hypogenitalism - severe mental and motor delay - central obesity, hypertonia, and postnatal growth retardation - dysmorphic features: edematous hands and feet, tapered fingers, single palmar crease, and bilateral talipes - increased acylcarnitine and fatty acids The index patient also had a narrow forehead, full cheeks, downturned corners of the mouth, and large ears. (2012) used exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous c.665T-C transition in the EIF2S3 gene, resulting in an ile222-to-thr (I222T) substitution. Capillary sequencing confirmed the mutation, and it cosegregated with the disorder in the family. The variant was not found in 188 X chromosomes from Moroccan Jewish controls, in dbSNP132, in the 1000 Genomes data, or in more than 8,000 alleles in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project. Ile222 lies in the GTP-binding domain and is strictly conserved in animals. The authors expressed tagged mutant eIF2-gamma in HeLa cells. The mutant protein pulled down substantially less eIF2-beta, whereas eIF2-alpha binding was not impaired, indicating that the mutation disrupts formation of the eIF2 complex. Borck et al. (2012) also noted a V151L variant in EIF2S3 that an earlier large-scale resequencing project had reported in a family with X-linked intellectual disability. In yeast, the corresponding mutation (V210L) caused defects in growth, GCN4 expression, and start site selection, and overexpression of tRNAi-Met suppressed these defects. The authors considered a causative role for V151L plausible.

In the patient from family 4, they found a hemizygous c.324T-A transversion resulting in a ser108-to-arg (S108R) substitution. He had inherited it from his healthy mother, and his healthy brother could not be tested. The yeast equivalent of S108R (Asp167Arg) had no effect, and the authors interpreted S108R as a variant of unknown significance.

The affected males had intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, and facial dysmorphism. The mutation was found by exome sequencing, confirmed by capillary sequencing, and cosegregated with the disorder in the family. It was absent from 188 control X chromosomes of Moroccan Jewish origin, from dbSNP132, from the 1000 Genomes data, and from more than 8,000 alleles in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project. Ile222 lies in the GTP-binding domain and is strictly conserved in animals. In HeLa cells, the mutant eIF2-gamma bound substantially less eIF2-beta, whereas eIF2-alpha binding was unaffected, indicating that the mutation disrupts eIF2 complex formation. In yeast, mutations at the corresponding residue (val281) impaired eIF2-beta binding, increased GCN4 expression, and raised the UUG/AUG initiation ratio.
